name: Amira Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I don't really follow the AI stuff, so I might not be much use, but go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small family-run agency in a town with a lot of villages round it, and I drive my own old hatchback between calls. First call is Mrs Pryce at half seven, she's 91 and very particular about her porridge, then out to Mr Haldane on his farm, who lost his wife last year and mostly needs someone to make sure he eats. I do about ten calls a day, split into mornings and evenings, and I go home to my flat over the bakery in between. I'm still learning, to be honest, I only started eighteen months ago and I'm slow with the hoist. What wears me out is the driving, and the car, because it's always something with that car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's more or less what I'd guess would happen anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much, I'm not one for posting. If it came up at the office I'd say well, there you go, all that fuss. People round here don't trust that stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same worries as now. The agency pays mileage at a rate set years ago, and petrol has gone up, so every call to the farms costs me a bit. My car's eleven years old and the garage said the clutch is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, that's all. I'd get the clutch done in the new year out of savings, which takes about a month of my three months saved. Then I'd try to build it back up by not going on the trip to the coast with my sister in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried about money, same as always. Not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the clutch costs a month of savings, what's the next thing that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing a client. If one of the farm calls goes into a home, I lose that hour and it's not always replaced. Mrs Pryce's son keeps talking about moving her nearer to him, and she's two calls a day for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you asked the agency about the mileage rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mentioned it to Gwen, she owns the agency, and she said she can't afford to change it with what the council pays her. I believe her, she's not a bad boss. It's just the way it is.

say: I'd keep it **low-key**: all that fuss, and people round here don't trust it anyway.
I'm **not one for posting**, so I'd only say it if it came up.
think: I keep the **same worries** as now: old mileage rates and rising petrol.
My **eleven-year-old car** needs a clutch, and that's a month of savings gone.
do: Pay for the **clutch** in the new year out of savings.
Skip the **summer trip** with her sister to rebuild the savings.
Carry on with the **same ten calls** a day.
feel: **Worried** about money, as always, but **not about AI**.
S0.quote: My car's eleven years old and the garage said the clutch is going.
fieldNote: Her pressures are **car costs** and a mileage rate that hasn't moved in years.
Losing a **single client** to a care home would cut her hours.
She defends her **boss**, seeing the council's pay as the real limit.

steps.text: Pay for the car's new clutch from savings in January
Skip the summer coast trip with her sister
Rebuild savings to three months by autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. So the office side. I'm out in the car all day, so that's not really me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who should worry, not us. Out loud I'd probably say I'm glad I do a real job with my hands. I'd not want to sound like I'm gloating, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means Gwen might sell up. The big agencies would have computers doing their rotas and their bills, and they'd be cheaper, and Gwen's already tired. If a big company bought us, I'd have new managers, apps, and probably more calls squeezed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put while Gwen's there. If they made me use an app on my phone, I'd ask Leanne in the office to show me twice and I'd write it down. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe forty, in case the new company changed my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my job exactly, more scared of things changing around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Leanne to show you twice. What makes new apps hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't like it. I pressed the wrong thing on the old timesheet app and it said I'd missed a call I'd done. Took three weeks to sort my pay. Paper never did that to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a big company bought Gwen's agency, would you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it six months. If they cut the farm calls short, I'd look at the other small agency on the far side of town. There are a few of us still, so there's somewhere to go.

say: It's the **office people** who should worry, not carers like me.
I'm glad I do a real job with **my hands**, without sounding like I'm gloating.
think: The owner might **sell up** to a cheaper big agency that runs on computers.
A new owner would mean **apps** and **more calls** squeezed into my day.
do: Stay at the agency while the **owner** is still running it.
Put about **forty a month** extra aside in case hours change.
Give a new owner **six months** before trying the other small agency.
feel: **Uneasy** about change around her rather than fearing for her own job.
S1.quote: I pressed the wrong thing on the old timesheet app and it said I'd missed a call I'd done.
fieldNote: She fears **ownership change** more than the technology itself.
A past **timesheet app** error cost her three weeks of pay hassle.
Sees **another small agency** nearby as a safe exit if needed.

steps.text: Put an extra forty a month into savings
Stay with the agency while the current owner runs it
Wait six months after any takeover before switching agencies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2031 that can do what I do. Well. That's not long, is it? I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and somebody should stop it. I'd sign whatever's going round. At work, I'd say what everyone would say: my old people won't stand for it. A 91-year-old woman I visit would throw her porridge at a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out of work by about 2031 and I've got nothing else. I left school early, I've done shop work and this. If robots can wash and dress people and the councils can pay less for them, Gwen couldn't compete even if she wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could, cancel the gym I never go to, and get my savings up from three months to six by 2030. I'd ask my sister if I could move in with her if it came to it. I don't know what I'd train in, honestly, because everything with hands would be going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everything with hands would be going too. Is there anything you'd look at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something where people have to see a face, like a receptionist at the doctor's. But the thinking AI would have that by 2028, wouldn't it? I really don't know, that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, Saima. She's a dental nurse, so she'd be worried for herself too. We'd sit in her kitchen and work out what we'd do if both of us lost our jobs.

say: It's **wrong**, somebody should stop it, and I'd sign whatever's going round.
The **old people** won't stand for robots washing them.
think: I'd be **out of work** by about 2031 with nothing else to fall back on.
If councils pay less for robots, a **small agency** couldn't compete.
do: Cancel the **gym** and push savings from three to **six months** by 2030.
Ask her sister about **moving in** together if it comes to that.
Sign every **petition** going round against it.
S2.quote: My old people won't stand for it. A 91-year-old woman I visit would throw her porridge at a robot.
fieldNote: Expects to be **out of work** by 2031 and sees no alternative path.
Can't name a **retraining option** because hands-on and desk work both look exposed.
Her safety net is **family**, a sister who works as a dental nurse.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and save toward six months by 2030
Ask her sister about moving in together if needed
Sign the petitions against robot care going round

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then robots around 2034. A bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to sort it out properly, and the government ought to look after the carers. I'd not make a fuss about it, though. I'd let the people who understand it argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd still lose the job around 2034, but I'd be 35 and maybe I'd have found something. Five years is enough to get my savings up and maybe do a course, even though I hate courses. I'd at least see it coming, which is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, save forty a month more, and maybe in a year or two look at a course, something like a healthcare assistant certificate at the college so I could work in the hospital. I wouldn't do it online, I'd do it in a room. I'd wait to see what other carers did first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. But it's a worry I could carry around, not one that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what other carers did. What if they wait too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd all be stuck together, I suppose. That's a fair point. Maybe I'd go with Leanne from the office if she's doing a course, I'd do it if she did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for you at work between 2031 and 2034, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the office side goes, so Gwen and Leanne are working with a computer that plans everything. I'd still be in the car going to the farm calls. Maybe I'd be glad of a few quiet years, honestly.

say: We've got time to **sort it out**, and government ought to look after carers.
I'd **not make a fuss**; I'd let people who understand it argue.
think: I'd still **lose the job** around 2034, but at 35 I might have something else.
Five years means I'd **see it coming**, which is something.
do: Save **forty a month** more and keep working as now.
Consider a **healthcare assistant** certificate at the college in a year or two.
Wait to see what **other carers** do before signing up.
feel: **Worried**, but a worry she can carry rather than one that keeps her awake.
S3.quote: I'd still be in the car going to the farm calls. Maybe I'd be glad of a few quiet years, honestly.
fieldNote: Five years makes her open to a **course**, but only in a classroom.
Admits waiting on others could leave everyone **stuck together**.
Would follow a **colleague** onto a course rather than go alone.

steps.text: Add forty a month to savings while working as now
Look at a college healthcare assistant certificate in a year or two
Wait to see whether colleagues sign up for courses first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots by 2039. I'd be 40. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's ten years off and there's no point panicking. If anyone asked, I'd say the government's got time to sort it, so they'd better. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd tell myself I've got time, and I'd probably not do much for a few years. The end's the same though, isn't it? I'd be 40 and in the same spot, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, get the car sorted, build the savings up slowly. Maybe in four or five years, once I'd seen what was happening, I'd do the healthcare assistant course. I'd probably wait to see if Gwen keeps going, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine on the surface. Underneath it's still there, like a dentist appointment you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end's the same. Does that bother you more or less than the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, because I'd have a bit of money behind me by then. But in a way it's worse, because I know I'd leave it too late. I always do. I left the clutch too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get you moving earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Gwen sat me down and said, here's what's going to happen to the agency. I'd listen to her. I wouldn't listen to the news.

say: It's **ten years off**, so there's no point panicking.
The government has **time to sort it**, so they'd better.
think: I'd tell myself I have time and **do little** for a few years.
The **end is the same**: I'd be 40 and in the same spot, just later.
do: Keep the **car** running and build savings up slowly.
Revisit the **healthcare assistant** course in four or five years.
Watch whether the **owner** keeps the agency going.
feel: Fine on the surface, but the worry sits underneath like a **dentist appointment**.
S4.quote: I know I'd leave it too late. I always do. I left the clutch too late.
fieldNote: Openly expects to **leave it too late**, as with her car's clutch.
Would act on her **boss's word**, not on the news.
Ten years lowers the **urgency** but not her sense that the job ends.

steps.text: Build savings slowly while keeping the car running
Wait to hear the owner's plans for the agency
Revisit the healthcare assistant course in four or five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Robots in 2031 and me with nothing else and no qualifications. What would help is somebody telling us plainly what's coming and a course in a real classroom near here, paid, so I could still pay rent while I did it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the villages. Some of the old people in the villages see nobody but me all day. A robot can bring a dinner, but Mr Haldane would just stop talking.

headlineQuote: Some of the old people in the villages see nobody but me all day.
portrait: A 27-year-old care worker at a **small family agency**, driving her own old car to village calls.
Left school early, eighteen months in, **slow with the hoist** and wary of apps.
Pragmatic and quiet; she **defends her boss** and blames council pay, not people.
AI Plateau and Steady Disruption worry her through **car costs** and a possible agency sale.
In the AGI pictures she expects to **lose the job** and has no clear second path.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots by 2031 and no qualifications to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid classroom course** nearby so she could keep paying rent.
